enrichment.short_title: Rutty Pool reinsurance rights after member insolvency
key_facts: Several Lloyd's and insurance companies sought court directions on their rights under the Rutty Pool, an underwriting pool managed by ME Rutty Underwriting Agency from 1962 to 1967.
North Atlantic Insurance Co Ltd (NAIC) and Australian Foundation Group (AFG) were insolvent; solvent pool members contended insolvent members' external reinsurance recoveries belonged to the pool.
The Rutty Agency was dissolved in 2000 and its authority to collect reinsurance for pool years had been cancelled in 1996-1997.
Disputes centred on whether mutual net-accounting obligations survived agency termination and whether insolvency invalidated several rights to pursue external reinsurers.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial court reference for directions on contested questions arising from a longstanding insurance pool run-off.
enrichment.outcome: On disputed points NAIC and AFG succeeded; the court held insolvent pool members could pursue external reinsurance recoveries severally.
enrichment.ratio: Once the Rutty Agency ceased acting for the pool, each pool member retained a several right to recover from external reinsurers; mutual net accounting and any Satanita-contract restrictions did not survive termination of the agency, and the British Eagle principle prevents contractual arrangements that would divert an insolvent member's assets away from its general creditors.
legal_issues: Whether external reinsurance recoveries were held on trust for the pool
Effect of termination of the Rutty Agency on mutual accounting obligations
Whether subrogation or unjust enrichment gave solvent members proprietary rights to insolvent members' reinsurance claims
Application of British Eagle to pool netting arrangements in insolvency

linked_authorities.name: British Eagle International Air Lines Ltd v Compagnie Nationale Air France
Napier v Hunter

confidence.notes: Long technical insurance judgment with clear conclusion favouring insolvent pool members on disputed points.

enrichment.short_title: School admission appeal panel judicial review
key_facts: Two families sought judicial review after Cardiff's admission appeal panel refused places at Rhydypenau Primary School for 2002-2003, citing class-size prejudice.
The panel found the council had failed to consider individual circumstances but concluded a reasonable authority would still not have admitted the children.
Parents argued the panel misapplied Schedule 24 paragraph 12, gave inadequate reasons, ignored lateness-for-school concerns, and acted unfairly in the Khundakji case.
Both children were ultimately placed at other schools after unsuccessful appeals.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of independent school admission appeal panel decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Both claims dismissed; permission to appeal refused.
enrichment.ratio: A finding that an admission authority erred in implementing arrangements does not automatically require a place to be offered under paragraph 12; the panel's task was whether refusal was unreasonable in the light of the admission arrangements, following Hounslow, and its reasons and treatment of lateness and Convention arguments were lawful.
legal_issues: Construction of Schedule 24 paragraph 12 in class-size prejudice appeals
Whether legal error by the admission authority compelled the panel to offer places
Adequacy of reasons for refusing appeals
Procedural fairness where head teacher evidence was challenged

linked_authorities.name: School Admission Appeals Panel v London Borough of Hounslow
R v Birmingham City Council, ex p B
Oxfordshire County Council v GB

confidence.notes: Full judgment read; detailed treatment of education admissions framework and all grounds of challenge.

enrichment.short_title: Validity of EIC bonus share issue
key_facts: EIC Services Ltd issued bonus shares on 15 December 1999 paid up from its share premium account following rapid share issues earlier in 1999.
Claimants argued the bonus issue was invalid because many allottees held unpaid shares and no shareholder resolution approved the issue.
The company had been used as a vehicle for internet-related investments after acquisition by Spickernell and Bryson in mid-1999.
Preliminary questions were tried on payment status of earlier shares, shareholder approval, and whether defects rendered the bonus shares void.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Preliminary issues trial in Chancery proceedings on validity of a December 1999 bonus share issue.
enrichment.outcome: Bonus issue held irregular but not void; unpaid allottees' shares treated as not paid up where section 35A did not apply.
enrichment.ratio: Failure to issue bonus shares only against fully paid shares and absence of shareholder approval made the December 1999 bonus issue irregular, but those defects did not render the issue void where section 35A of the Companies Act 1985 applied.
legal_issues: Whether bonus shares could be allotted to holders of unpaid shares
Whether shareholder approval was required under the articles and Duomatic principle
Whether irregular allotment was void for mistake or breach of articles
Scope of section 35A in validating defective allotments

confidence.notes: Very long judgment; core preliminary conclusions at paragraph 226 are clear though some related trial issues remained outstanding.

enrichment.short_title: Judicial review of fur farming compensation scheme
key_facts: Ten former English mink fur farmers, all members of the Fur Breeders Association, challenged the 2002 compensation order made under the Fur Farming Prohibition Act 2000.
The scheme paid £40 per breeding female with no payment for males and no premium for higher-value breeds, and reduced payments if farmers continued trading after set dates.
Farmers who pelted stock before November could not realise full pelt value yet faced reduced breeding-stock compensation under the sliding scale.
DEFRA had consulted animal welfare groups opposed to any compensation as well as farmers and the NFU.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of a statutory compensation scheme made by order in council.
enrichment.outcome: Compensation provisions for residual breeding stock held unlawful; court invited submissions on whether to quash the whole order or only Schedule 1(2)(a) and Schedule 3.
enrichment.ratio: The breeding-stock compensation formula was irrational and unfair because it excluded males, ignored premium breeds, and penalised farmers who continued in business on a sliding scale that conflicted with earlier assurances and Browns' valuation assumptions, infringing Article 1 Protocol 1 rights as well as common-law fairness requirements.
legal_issues: Whether section 5(4) limited consultation to fur farmers exclusively
Whether views opposing any compensation could lawfully be taken into account
Rationality and fairness of omitting male mink and breed differentials
Legitimate expectation arising from MAFF's February 2001 letter

linked_authorities.name: Lithgow v United Kingdom
Papachelas v Greece
Cullinane v British Rema Manufacturing Co Ltd

confidence.notes: Detailed administrative review with clear findings of unlawfulness on breeding-stock compensation.

enrichment.short_title: Patent damages causation at enquiry stage
key_facts: Coflexip's patent for vertical flexible pipe laying had been held valid and infringed by Stolt's use of the Seaway Falcon.
At the damages enquiry Stolt applied to strike out Coflexip's claims for lost profits and price reductions for inadequate pleading of causation.
Jacob J ordered repleading on the basis that Coflexip had to show the patented process was causative of winning contracts, not merely that but for infringement it would have obtained them.
Coflexip appealed while accepting its pleading needed improvement but disputing the judge's legal direction.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal from strike-out/repleading orders in a patent damages enquiry.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; repleading required but not constrained to the judge's causation view; no order for costs.
enrichment.ratio: It was premature at the pleading stage to decide whether a patentee must prove customers wanted the infringing process to award loss-of-profit damages; Coflexip's approach based on United Horse Shoe and related authorities was at least arguable and should be tested once facts are found.
legal_issues: Causation for patent damages based on diverted contracts
Whether infringer can rely on non-infringing alternatives to defeat lost-profit claims
Appropriateness of resolving causation before factual enquiry
Pleading adequacy for price-reduction damages

linked_authorities.name: General Tire and Rubber Co v Firestone Tyre and Rubber Co Ltd
The United Horse Shoe and Nail Co Ltd v John Stewart & Co
Gerber Garment Technology Inc v Lectra Systems Ltd
Kuwait Airways Corp v Iraqi Airways Co
Gallagher Electronics Ltd v Donaghys Electrics Ltd

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment on interlocutory patent damages law with detailed authority review.

enrichment.short_title: Planning challenge to caravan enforcement and refusal
key_facts: Mr Blackburn bought land at The Paddock, Whaplode St Catherine, lived in a caravan there, and applied for outline planning permission for a dwelling.

South Holland District Council refused planning permission for countryside incursion and flood-risk reasons and served an enforcement notice alleging unauthorised residential use of the land as a caravan site.
Blackburn appealed the enforcement notice on ground (c) only and the planning refusal on merits and Article 8 grounds.
An inspector upheld the enforcement notice and dismissed the planning appeal after a November 2002 hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Combined section 289 permission application and section 288 statutory challenge to a planning inspector's decisions.
enrichment.outcome: Both applications refused; claimant ordered to pay the Secretary of State's costs summarily assessed at £4,500.
enrichment.ratio: The inspector lawfully found a change of use to residential caravan occupation had occurred and correctly balanced countryside policy, flood risk, and personal housing need; the court cannot rehear planning merits absent error of law.
legal_issues: Whether use as a home in a caravan constituted breach of planning control
Correctness of inspector's countryside and settlement boundary assessment
Whether personal need for affordable housing outweighed policy objections
Article 8 balance in refusing planning permission

confidence.notes: Short planning judgment with straightforward refusal on conventional grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Article 6 and automatic British citizenship claims
key_facts: Peter Harrison, born in New Zealand in 1946, claimed automatic British citizenship through his father's alleged birth on a British-registered ship in 1897.
A Home Office ministerial letter rejected the claim for lack of evidence, noting an Adelaide birth certificate inconsistent with the ship-birth account.
Harrison sought judicial review and an independent tribunal, arguing citizenship entitlement was a civil right under Article 6 ECHR.
Permission to appeal was limited to whether recognition as a citizen engages Article 6.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with limited permission from refusal of permission to apply for judicial review of a Home Office citizenship letter.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no order as to costs.
enrichment.ratio: Article 6 is not engaged because the minister's letter did not determine Harrison's legal right to citizenship; where statute confers automatic citizenship on proof of facts, any dispute is for the courts by declaration rather than administrative determination.
legal_issues: Whether entitlement to British citizenship is a civil right under Article 6(1)
Whether the Secretary of State makes a determination when rejecting an automatic citizenship claim
Construction of birth aboard a registered ship under the 1948 Act
Need for an independent citizenship tribunal

linked_authorities.name: Ferrazzini v Italy
Maaouia v France
Karassev v Switzerland
R (Alconbury Developments Ltd) v Secretary of State for the Environment

confidence.notes: Clear Court of Appeal reasoning on Article 6 scope in automatic citizenship cases.

enrichment.short_title: Libel meaning in Nlite laser withdrawal letter
key_facts: ICN Photonics manufactured the Nlite laser wrinkle-treatment system; Dr Patterson wrote to salon customers withdrawing his services from Elite Health and Beauty.
The letter criticised the salon owner and said Patterson would not risk his reputation using the Nlite laser, citing distributor bankruptcy and low consumer satisfaction.
ICN Photonics sued for libel and slander of goods; Popplewell J held the words capable of both defamatory and disparaging meanings.
Patterson appealed the defamation meaning ruling while agreeing part of the slander-of-goods pleading should be narrowed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal from a meaning ruling under CPR Part 53 in libel and slander-of-goods proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; defamation claim struck out on meaning but slander-of-goods claim proceeds with agreed amendment.
enrichment.ratio: The withdrawal letter was not reasonably capable of meaning that the manufacturer knew the laser required medical supervision yet allowed unsupervised salon use; criticism of the health authority's supervision did not impute reprehensible conduct to the manufacturer.
legal_issues: Whether words disparaging a product also defame its manufacturer
Natural and ordinary meaning of criticism about medical supervision
Appellate intervention in inclusive meaning rulings
Scope of slander-of-goods claim after defamation struck out

linked_authorities.name: Hope Technical Developments Ltd v British Broadcasting Corporation
Gillick v Brook Advisory Centre
Griffiths v Benn

confidence.notes: Focused interlocutory defamation judgment with clear outcome on pleaded meaning.

key_facts: Arbuthnot Fund Managers sued former executive director Nigel Rawlings to enforce twelve-month post-termination restraints in his 1998 service agreement.
Rawlings had sold A&R Equity to Secure Trust in 1994 and managed clients representing about 42% of the firm's funds under management.
He resigned on 11 November 2002 alleging constructive dismissal and gave limited undertakings pending trial.
Heppel J granted interim injunctions restricting client solicitation broadly similar to clauses 15.1.1 and 15.1.2.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Interlocutory appeal from interim injunction enforcing restrictive covenants pending expedited trial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; injunctions narrowed by construing and deleting overly wide restraint terms.
enrichment.ratio: Post-termination client restraints must be construed in context of protecting goodwill and business connections; at this stage clauses restraining any person introduced at any time, any client with whom the employee had knowledge, or prospective clients known only to colleagues were plainly too wide, though narrower twelve-month dealing restrictions could stand.
legal_issues: Construction of non-solicitation and non-dealing covenants in a financial services employment contract
Whether restraints were void for unreasonable breadth at interlocutory stage
Effect of alleged constructive dismissal on enforceability
Appropriate interim relief under American Cyanamid principles

linked_authorities.name: American Cyanamid Co v Ethicon Ltd
Home Counties Dairies Ltd v Skilton
Rock Refrigeration Ltd v Jones

confidence.notes: Detailed construction-based appellate judgment modifying interim restraints.

key_facts: Dr Suressh Deman, a US citizen of Indian origin, was a probationary lecturer at Queen's University Belfast and an AUT member from 1994 to 1995.
He complained the AUT failed to investigate local branch discrimination and refused legal aid for his employment claims against the university.
The employment tribunal criticised AUT officials' handling but dismissed race discrimination and victimisation claims for lack of inferential evidence.
The EAT upheld dismissal; the Court of Appeal found the tribunal's reasoning legally deficient.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Employment Appeal Tribunal dismissal of race discrimination and victimisation claims against a trade union.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision set aside and case remitted for rehearing with case-management directions.
enrichment.ratio: The tribunal's conclusion that there was no evidence from which to infer race discrimination was wrong given its own findings of less favourable treatment and mishandled legal-aid decisions; it also failed to give adequate reasons and did not properly address unconscious discrimination following Nagarajan.
legal_issues: Drawing inferences of race discrimination from primary facts
Adequacy of employment tribunal reasons in discrimination cases
Conscious versus unconscious racial discrimination after Nagarajan
Jurisdiction over events in Northern Ireland as background only

linked_authorities.name: King v Great Britain-China Centre
Qureshi v Victoria University of Manchester
Nagarajan v London Regional Transport
Anya v University of Oxford

confidence.notes: Full Court of Appeal judgment with detailed critique of tribunal reasoning on inference and reasons.
